terms.gloss: skim flat stones over the water
terms.grammar: jaculor, jaculārī, jaculātus sum with the accusative of what is thrown
terms.comment: A description, after the game as Minucius Felix describes it: boys on the beach at Ostia picking up a flat sherd or stone smoothed by the waves and sending it low over the water to skip (testārum in mare jaculātiōnibus lūdere). His own verb, testam super undās inrotāre, is found only in this passage (Lewis & Short), and we have found no other ancient name for the game, so the description stands. Summa aqua, the surface of the water, is Vergil’s (G. 1.369 summā nantīs in aquā). For splashing, see “splash”.

phrases.latin: Plānam testam ēlige; ea per summam aquam exsiliet.
phrases.english: Pick a flat stone; that one will skip across the water.
How many times did your stone bounce? — Three times!
Let’s throw pebbles in the water.

phrases.latin: puerōs vidēmus certātim gestientēs testārum in mare jaculātiōnibus lūdere
phrases.english: we see boys eagerly vying with one another at their game of skimming stones on the sea

phrases.latin: Is sē in puerīs victōrem ferēbat, cujus testa et prōcurreret longius et frequentius exsilīret.
phrases.english: Among the boys the winner was the one whose stone both ran on furthest and bounced most often.

sources: Lewis & Short: testa · Lewis & Short: jaculor · Lewis & Short: irroto · Lewis & Short: exsilio
